title: Breaking an oath
hookLine: the expiation for a broken oath is feeding ten poor people (5:89)

lines: A BILL, PAYABLE TO THE HUNGRY.
cards: Wallahi. By God. It turns up in plenty of arguments about who ate the last samosa.
Wallahi I didn't. Wallahi I'll be there in five minutes. It slips out so easily it barely registers.

Then there's the other kind: the oath sworn in earnest, in anger. By God, I will never speak to you again. What does the Qur'an do with someone who swore something like that and now wishes they hadn't?
It doesn't shrug. It doesn't trap them either. It hands them a bill, payable to the hungry.

teach.h: LAGHW — THE OATHS THAT SLIP OUT.
teach.b: Surah five, verse eighty-nine, draws a line between two kinds of oath. The first is laghw, idle talk: oaths that fall out of your mouth without meaning to bind anything.

Allah, the verse says, doesn't take you to task for those. A report in Bukhari has Aishah explaining them as the everyday no, by God, and yes, by God, of casual speech. The second kind is sworn deliberately.
Break that one, and there's a cost.
In Pickthall's words: “The expiation thereof is the feeding of ten of the needy,” with the average of what you feed your own family. Or clothing ten people.
Or freeing a slave, an act the Qur'an names as an expiation in other verses too. If none of that is possible, three days of fasting. The word is kaffarah.

Arabic dictionaries give its root, k-f-r, the sense of covering over, the way a farmer covers seed with soil. A kaffarah covers a broken word, not by pretending it wasn't broken, but by laying something good on top of it.

teach.h: DO THE BETTER THING, AND PAY.
teach.b: A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says that if someone swears to do something, then sees that something else is better, they should do the better thing and pay the expiation.

So in the hadith's logic, an oath never to speak to a brother isn't a cage: the better thing is the phone call, and the expiation is the meal for ten. Near its end, the verse tells believers to guard their oaths.
The simplest way to guard them is to swear fewer.

how: Muslims who break a deliberate oath pay kaffarah, often by feeding ten needy people or giving the equivalent through a mosque or charity; if they can't, they fast three days. Some teachers also discourage swearing by God in everyday talk.

o: a fast kept to undo any sin at all
a fine paid to a judge for lying
an expiation that covers a broken oath

s: every casual "by God" is a binding oath
the verse says Allah doesn't take you to task for idle oaths, laghw.
a hadith says to break an oath when something better appears, and expiate

games.q: you swore by God you'd never speak to your brother again. now you see that making peace is better. what does the hadith say?
o: keep the oath. an oath is an oath.
do the better thing, and pay the expiation.
nothing. oaths sworn in anger don't count.
games.why: the Prophet said that if you swear and then see something better, do the better thing and expiate the oath. go call him, and feed ten people.

practice: Think back over the last week: where did a big word, by God, I swear, I'll never, stand in for a plain yes or no?
Then let one person you could feed come to mind, a friend, a neighbor, a food bank, and let the two thoughts sit together.

wordCard.voice: Kaffarah. Expiation: the covering of a broken oath, by feeding ten people, clothing them, freeing someone, or fasting three days. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: expiation, from k-f-r, to cover over.

carryVoice: Your line: swear less. A plain yes or no is enough. Day three hundred ninety-five, done.
